questions.q: (a) Describe an experiment with a source, a GM tube and absorbers to identify the radiation emitted [3]. (b) Graph on the sheet: find the half-life [2]. (c) Explain why gamma is used to sterilise surgical instruments but alpha is not [2]. (d) Distinguish contamination from irradiation [1].
questions.a: (a) measure background count (1); measure count with paper, then aluminium, then lead between source and tube (1); where the count drops to background identifies the type (1); (b) read time for activity to halve, e.g. 40 s (2); (c) gamma penetrates packaging and kills microbes (1); alpha cannot pass through packaging (1); (d) contamination: source on or in the object; irradiation: exposed to radiation from outside (1)
questions.model: Teacher sets out (b) on the graph: start at 600, halve to 300, read across and down.

questions.q: Explain why alpha sources are most dangerous inside the body but least dangerous outside.
questions.a: Strongly ionising so damages cells inside (1); outside, stopped by dead skin/air (1); inside, nothing stops it reaching living cells (1)

questions.q: A sample has 1/16 of its original activity after 20 years. Find the half-life.

questions.q: Which radiation is used in smoke alarms and why?
questions.a: Alpha: strongly ionising, short range, stopped by smoke
